title: Reporting Module — Scheduled Reports from Saved Dashboards
overview: A Sand Platform capability, surfaced in SandGen (Sand Generation) first, that turns a saved dashboard into a report delivered by email on a repeating schedule. The person picks a report type, picks a source dashboard, chooses the sites/devices/portfolio it covers, picks PDF or Excel, sets a day and time in a declared time zone, lists recipient addresses, and switches it on; the platform then renders and sends the file and records every run. Manual report creation already ships and is unchanged. Out of scope: customer-formula reports, mobile, any delivery route but email, billing documents, and any report content a dashboard cannot already show. PRD v1 dated 2026-09-08, owner Mohamed Moanes, with a companion annex (PRD-reporting-module-v1-ANNEX) that authors the field dictionary, the screen state matrix and the eleven failure states. Source PDFs carry no delivery date by deliberate decision; they state order instead.

requirements.description: A reporting setup page exists as a distinct page in the Sand Generation shell.
acceptance_criteria: The page is application-resident, not platform-level

requirements.description: The reporting setup page presents the three report types as tabs: system, my reports, shared.
acceptance_criteria: The three types must not be invented or altered

requirements.description: Each type tab lists the reports available in that type.
The report editor offers a single-select source picker over saved dashboards, default or customer-built, and a report sources from exactly one of them.
The chosen source dashboard's name is displayed on screen.
The source dashboard's name is printed in the produced file.
Coverage kind is chosen as exactly one of: particular sites, particular devices, or the whole portfolio.
acceptance_criteria: The three coverage kinds must not be invented or altered

requirements.description: The coverage picker offers only the scopes the chosen source dashboard permits, and re-offers when the source changes.
acceptance_criteria: Named in the PRD as the hardest interaction in the module

requirements.description: An out-of-scope coverage request is refused where the data is fetched, not where it is displayed.
Output format is chosen as PDF or Excel.
acceptance_criteria: The two formats must not be invented or altered

requirements.description: Each output format is a registered renderer rather than a branch in report code, so a third format later costs a registration.
When the format is PDF, the person chooses one of: diagrams and tables, diagrams only, tables only.
acceptance_criteria: The three PDF content choices must not be invented or altered

requirements.description: The produced PDF contains only the content kind that was chosen.
In Excel output, each dashboard panel becomes its own sheet.
In Excel output, a diagram panel contributes the values behind the chart rather than a picture, so a dashboard with no tables still produces a usable file.
Report values resolve through the same calculation path the dashboard uses, for the report's own period, with no second calculation path added.
The portfolio coverage option is shown only where the source dashboard's scope can be expressed at portfolio level; otherwise it is not shown.
A portfolio-level request made by identifier where the source does not support it is refused.
A report carries a repeating schedule expressed as a date and a time.
The schedule runs while the report is active and stops when the report is switched off.
A schedule's time zone is explicitly declared as part of the schedule, never implicit.
The declared time zone is stated on screen beside the schedule.
acceptance_criteria: A report set for 07:00 arrives at 07:00 somewhere specific

requirements.description: A report can be generated once, on demand, from the interface.
An on-demand generation produces exactly one file and one delivery.
Each report has an active switch in the interface.
Switching a report off stops delivery, and switching it on resumes it without backfilling runs missed while it was off.
Delivery recipients are entered as a list of email addresses.
A recipient need not belong to a platform user.
acceptance_criteria: No recipient-side permission check exists, by design

requirements.description: Email leaves through the platform's mail abstraction, never a direct connection to a mail provider.
Every generated file is produced through the platform's storage abstraction.
A generated file is kept for a retention period stated in the product rather than left to infrastructure.
acceptance_criteria: PRD marks the duration [NEEDS INPUT] — see constraints

requirements.description: A run history is available per report.
A run history entry shows when the run happened, what it covered, which file it produced, who received it, and whether it succeeded.
Every delivery is recorded before sending, because email cannot be recalled.
A failed run records the reason for the failure.
A failed run tells the report's creator.
Retries are bounded, and after the last attempt the report goes inactive rather than failing silently forever.
Every action is gated on a privilege, never on a role name, so a client creating or renaming roles later breaks nothing.
A dispatch resolves its data against one declared authority, resolved at the run and never cached from creation.
acceptance_criteria: Rests on the PRD's one blocking question

requirements.description: The declared authority is named in the produced file, so a reader can tell whose view of the portfolio they hold.
When the declared authority loses access to a covered site, the next run does not send, the report goes inactive, and the reason is recorded.
The produced file is never trimmed to what remains visible when access narrows — a report that silently shrinks is worse than one that stops.
Deleting a dashboard first names every scheduled report depending on it, and how many.
Deleting a dashboard that has dependent reports anyway requires a second deliberate action.
Reports whose source dashboard was deleted go inactive with the reason recorded, and never send an empty or broken file.
Editing a source dashboard takes effect on the next run, with no notification, because an edit is normal.
The produced file records the source dashboard's last-changed time so a reader can see why two periods differ.
Report definitions, generated files and run history are scoped to one client account and unreadable from another by any route, structurally rather than by query filter.
Where a person lacks a privilege the control is hidden, not greyed out.
acceptance_criteria: The hidden-not-disabled rule must not be invented or altered

requirements.description: The layout leaves no hole where a hidden control would have been.

Quantities with kilo/mega/giga multiples are stored in base units and scaled only when displayed, including inside the PDF and Excel files, with the unit label derived from the value rather than stored separately.
The report lists support choosing which columns are shown.
The report lists support filtering.
The report lists support searching.
The report lists support paging.
The report lists provide a page-size selector.
The report lists show a "showing X of Y" counter.
The three report type tabs carry count badges.
The manual report creation that already shipped is unchanged by this release; scheduled reports are added alongside it.
A report editor screen exists, covering coverage, format, schedule and recipients.
acceptance_criteria: Named in Design Deliverables screen inventory

requirements.description: An entry point from a dashboard offers "make a report from this".
acceptance_criteria: Named in Design Deliverables screen inventory

requirements.description: The PDF layout is designed in each of its three content variants.
acceptance_criteria: A design surface even though nobody clicks it

requirements.description: The Excel workbook structure is designed.
acceptance_criteria: A design surface even though nobody clicks it

requirements.description: The delivery email is designed as its own surface, not left to a default.
acceptance_criteria: Explicitly called a fifth surface needing a design, not a default

requirements.description: A report has a required name, unique within its type and client account.
Where two reports share a name, neither is ever shown without something distinguishing them.
A report has an optional free-text description.
A report's type is set at creation, and changing it afterwards is a privileged action.
The active switch is off by default when a report is created.
A report has a required period field defining the window it covers, defaulting from the source dashboard's saved default and overridable.
A schedule's kind is chosen as repeating or one-time.
A repeating schedule requires a start date.
A repeating schedule requires a time of day.
A repeating schedule requires a repeat interval.
acceptance_criteria: PRD marks the offered set [NEEDS INPUT] — see open decisions

requirements.description: At least one recipient address is required before a report can be switched on.
Whether a recipient is inside or outside the organization is derived from the address and gates the send-outside-the-organization privilege.

The module introduces exactly seven privileges: see system reports, create a private report, share a report, schedule and switch off, switch off another person's report, send outside the organization, and read run history.
acceptance_criteria: The privilege table must not be invented or altered

requirements.description: Nobody in the client account may change what a system report contains, at any role.
acceptance_criteria: Architect-proposed, flagged for confirmation in the PRD

requirements.description: Setup page empty state: a tab with no reports says so and offers the way to make one where the privilege allows; the system tab is never empty.
Setup page loading state: the tab shape and the count badges resolve first, the list after.
Setup page forbidden state: a person without the see-system privilege does not get the system tab at all — hidden, not empty.
Setup page error state: the list fails to load with a retry, and the tabs stay usable.
Setup page partial-data state: some reports show a "source unavailable" marker rather than the whole list failing.
Report editor empty state: a new report shows the source picker first, because every other field depends on it.
Report editor loading state: coverage options load after the source is chosen and are visibly pending.
Report editor forbidden state: controls the person lacks are absent, with no gap left in the layout.
Report editor error state: a save failure keeps every entered value, and nothing is silently discarded.
Report editor partial-data state: if the coverage list is only partly resolvable, show what resolved and name what did not.
Run history empty state: a report that has never run says so plainly, not as an error.
Run history loading state: newest first, paged.
Run history forbidden state: absent for a person without the read-history privilege.
Run history error state: a history that will not load does not block the report itself.
Run history partial state: a run mid-flight shows as running, not as failed.
Dashboard entry point loading state: inline.
Dashboard entry point forbidden state: hidden where the create privilege is absent.
Dashboard entry point error state: falls back to the setup page with the source pre-chosen.
Produced PDF empty state: a period with no readings produces a file that says there were no readings — never an empty page and never a silent success.
Produced PDF error state: a panel that cannot render leaves a stated placeholder, not a blank.
Produced PDF partial state: rendered panels appear and unrendered ones are named.
Produced Excel empty state: a sheet stating there were no readings, not an empty sheet.
Produced Excel error state: a panel that cannot resolve gets a sheet naming the problem.
Produced Excel partial state: resolved sheets appear and unresolved ones are named.
Delivery email error state: a failure never sends a partial email — nothing goes out, and the run records why.
Nothing in this module ever reports success for an artefact that is not there; silent non-delivery is a defect.
acceptance_criteria: The one rule across all seven surfaces

requirements.description: A generated file that exceeds the attachment ceiling fails the run before sending, with a stated reason, and the file is retained so somebody can retrieve it — never handed to a mail provider to drop.
When many schedules fire in the same minute, runs queue rather than being dropped; ordering is not guaranteed but delivery is.
acceptance_criteria: PRD marks concurrency [NEEDS INPUT] — see constraints

requirements.description: When a recipient address bounces, the run is recorded as delivered-with-failures, naming which addresses failed, and delivery to the others is not rolled back.
A one-time report requested twice in quick succession produces two runs, two files and two deliveries, and is not deduplicated.
Failure is made visible without the page becoming an incident dashboard.
acceptance_criteria: Named in Design Deliverables as the second hardest interaction

requirements.description: A run record stores coverage and period as resolved rather than as configured, because the two can differ if access narrowed.

use_cases: As an Asset Manager, have last week's portfolio summary in my inbox on Monday without opening Sand.
As an O&M Manager, send the same site report to the same three people weekly and stop rebuilding it.
As somebody in the client's Technical Office, produce one report now, for one site, with no schedule.
As an Owner or Admin, stop a shared report going to the wrong people without hunting for its author.
As anybody who set one up, find out that last night's report did not send, and why.
constraints: Out of scope: reports built on customer-defined formulas (the Formula Builder is postponed).
Out of scope: any mobile surface.
Out of scope: new report content — charts, figures or KPIs the platform cannot already show. Every report is a dashboard snapshot.
Out of scope: report building outside a dashboard. If a person wants what no dashboard shows, they build the dashboard first.
Out of scope: any delivery route other than email — no in-platform inbox, no download links, no file storage delivery.
Out of scope: billing documents and invoices.
Out of scope: output formats other than PDF and Excel.
Out of scope: recipient-side permission checks — recipients are email addresses, not platform users, so there is nobody to check. Named as the largest risk in the document.
Out of scope: editing or annotating a generated file.

Permission model uses the Admin Module's four roles (Owner, Admin, Engineer, Technician), NOT the eight commercial role names, and no mapping between the two lists is proposed. Every requirement is written against a privilege, never a role name.
Design must not invent: the three report types, the three coverage kinds, the two formats, the three PDF content choices, the privilege table, or the hidden-not-disabled rule.
Left to design: the setup page layout, how the tabs present, how the PDF variants look.
Depends on the Admin Module (private and shared reports mean nothing until each person has an account) — in user acceptance testing, not released.
Depends on the dashboard builders (they produce the sources) — in user acceptance testing, not released.
Depends on a working email route — Sand has a mail abstraction but no delivered email route.

[NEEDS INPUT — architecture] Whose authority renders a scheduled report, and what happens when it changes. Filed as the one blocking question; the private-report path can be built and the shared path cannot until it is answered.
[NEEDS INPUT — architecture] Does a time-triggered scheduler exist in platform-dev today? The core of this module is a timer and the architecture digest does not confirm one exists.
[NEEDS INPUT — architecture] Is there a delivered email route, or only the mail abstraction?
[NEEDS INPUT — architecture] Does a report definition live as configuration or in new tables?
[NEEDS INPUT — architecture] Where is a PDF or spreadsheet rendered, and does it run in the request path?
[NEEDS INPUT — architecture] How is the dispatch-low, measures-high dependency tension split?

[NEEDS INPUT — data nobody has] How many sites, devices, users and active scheduled reports should this be built for? A scheduler cannot be sized against an unknown number of reports all set for Monday at eight.
[NEEDS INPUT — data nobody has] How long is a generated file kept, and does any regulation apply? (bears on REQ-31)
[NEEDS INPUT — data nobody has] What is the attachment size ceiling before a mail provider refuses? (bears on REQ-105)
[NEEDS INPUT — data nobody has] How many concurrent runs must be supported? (bears on REQ-106)
[NEEDS INPUT — quality bars never specified] File retention, generation time, concurrent runs, uptime, accessibility, and expected volumes. Nothing was invented to fill them.
[NEEDS INPUT — commercial] Is this module Basic or Plus? Scheduling appears in neither published tier list.
[NEEDS INPUT — process] Who approves this PRD — Functional Lead, CTO, or both?
[NEEDS INPUT — user research] What reports do the three client teams actually build by hand today? The module is specified against a described need rather than a measured one.

No delivery date, target quarter or committed date appears in the PRD — a deliberate decision by the Product Manager on 2026-09-08. What is stated is order: nothing delivers until Sand has a working email route.
Every numeric target in Goals is marked proposed rather than measured; no baseline exists for anything today.
One designer is available and this module has already displaced the mobile app in the design queue.

unverified_prd_claims.claim: "As authority drops, controls are hidden, not greyed out, and the layout must not leave a hole where a hidden control would have been — the same rule the Admin Module and the dashboards use."

Requirement 26's list behaviours — column choosing, filtering, searching, paging, a page-size selector, a "showing X of Y" counter and count badges on tabs — are sourced from "Admin PRD", implying these patterns already exist there to be reused.
Requirement 25's base-unit storage with display-time scaling and derived labels is sourced from "Admin PRD", implying an existing convention.
"The manual report creation that already shipped is unchanged by this release." — asserts an existing shipped reporting surface in Sand Generation.
"Reporting in Sand Generation exists and works. What it does not do is repeat."
"Most of this already exists in Sand's shared code. The new parts are the report itself, the PDF and Excel writers, the timer, and the sending."

Five of six fundamental mechanisms are claimed reusable: the adapter pattern for mail and storage, the polymorphic domain hierarchy for scope, JSON parameterization, automatic CRUD resource generation, and schema-driven dynamic views.

"The Admin Module and the dashboard builders are in user acceptance testing, not released." The PRD itself flags that 09_shipped-state.md (2026-08-09) still records both as in progress, so the sources disagree.
"Sand has a mail abstraction but no delivered email route." Taken from PRD-notification-center-v5 and explicitly labelled a dependency to confirm rather than a fact to build on.
PRD-customizable-dashboards-v2 "already names 'the Report Creator' as the candidate consumer of the platform's composition model".
The Admin Module supplies four enforced roles — Owner, Admin, Engineer, Technician — and a later release lets a client create its own roles with chosen privileges.
The dashboard builders permit a saved dashboard's scope to be expressed at portfolio level in some cases but not others (Requirement 8 depends on this being inspectable).
A saved dashboard carries a "saved default" period that a report's period field can default from (Annex A field dictionary).
A dashboard exposes a last-changed time that the produced file can record (Requirement 22).
A dashboard is composed of "panels" that can be enumerated and classified as diagram or table, which Requirements 6 and 12 both depend on.
Deleting a dashboard is a flow owned by the dashboard builders that this module can insert a dependent-report warning into (Requirement 21).

open_decisions.decision: Is the schedule set on the report itself, or in a separate step?
options: On the report — schedule fields sit inline in the report editor alongside coverage, format and recipients
A separate step — the editor saves the report definition, and scheduling is a distinct screen or stage afterwards
open_decisions.recommended: On the report — schedule fields sit inline in the report editor alongside coverage, format and recipients
open_decisions.consequences: Inline matches the Product Manager's described flow (pick a report, say what it covers, pick a format, set a day and time, list who gets it, switch it on) and keeps one editor to design and one save to reason about; but the editor becomes long, and the annex already requires progressive disclosure because coverage cannot load until the source is chosen. A separate step shortens each screen and suits reusing one schedule across reports later, at the cost of a second save, a second set of five states, and a flow that no longer matches how the PRD describes the task.

open_decisions.decision: Is a schedule a property of one report, or a reusable object several reports can share?
options: A property of one report — each report owns its own schedule
A reusable object — a named schedule several reports attach to
open_decisions.recommended: A property of one report — each report owns its own schedule
open_decisions.consequences: The PRD proposes the first and says so explicitly. One-per-report needs no schedule library, no attach/detach UI and no answer to what happens when a shared schedule is edited or deleted. A reusable object would let a client change "Monday 07:00" once for nine reports, but adds a management surface nobody asked for and makes the blast radius of an edit invisible at the point of editing.

options: A stated set: daily, weekly, monthly
A stated set plus quarterly and yearly
A free recurrence builder (every N days/weeks/months, with weekday selection)
open_decisions.recommended: A stated set: daily, weekly, monthly
open_decisions.consequences: The Product Manager said "periodically" without naming a set, so this is genuinely unspecified. Three fixed intervals is a single select, testable in one check, and covers every scenario the PRD names (all five use cases are weekly or one-off). Adding quarterly and yearly is nearly free in the control but each needs a defined anchor day. A recurrence builder is a substantially larger design and interacts with the time-zone rule and with concurrency sizing, which is itself unanswered.

open_decisions.decision: Does run history sit on each report, or in one place for all of them?
options: On each report — history is a view within the report
One central place — a module-level history across all reports, filterable by report
Both — a central list plus a per-report view
open_decisions.recommended: On each report — history is a view within the report
open_decisions.consequences: Requirement 16 specifies "a run history per report", and per-report keeps the forbidden state simple (absent without the read-history privilege) and the error state contained (a history that will not load does not block the report). But the use case "find out that last night's report did not send" is answered badly by per-report history: the person must already know which report failed, and with nine reports that is nine places to look. A central place answers that directly and is where the "visible without alarming anyone" requirement naturally lives. Both is the most useful and the most to design and state-matrix.

open_decisions.decision: Does the entry point from a dashboard open the full setup page, or a short form?
options: A short form — a compact overlay capturing the minimum, with the source pre-chosen
The full setup page — navigate to the report editor with the source pre-chosen
open_decisions.recommended: A short form — a compact overlay capturing the minimum, with the source pre-chosen
open_decisions.consequences: A short form keeps the person on their dashboard and suits the "produce one report now, for one site, with no schedule" use case; but it needs a defined minimum field set, its own validation, and a defined path to the full editor for anything it omits — and the annex already specifies that its error state falls back to the setup page with the source pre-chosen, which means both surfaces exist either way. Navigating to the full editor adds no new surface and no second field set, at the cost of pulling the person out of the dashboard for what the PRD frames as a quick action.

open_decisions.decision: What does the recipient list look like at twenty addresses?
options: A chip/token field — addresses as removable tokens that wrap, with a scroll cap
A managed list — one row per address in a scrollable list with per-row remove and an add field
A textarea of addresses parsed on save
open_decisions.recommended: A managed list — one row per address in a scrollable list with per-row remove and an add field
open_decisions.consequences: A managed list is the only one of the three with somewhere to put per-address information, and two requirements need exactly that: inside-or-outside-the-organization is derived per address and gates a privilege (REQ-76), and a bounce is reported per address (REQ-107). Chips are compact and familiar but have no room for a per-address state or bounce marker, and twenty of them wrap into an unreadable block. A textarea is the cheapest to build and the worst here — it cannot show derived state at all, and it makes a typo in a portfolio recipient list invisible until after the file has left, which the PRD names as its largest risk.

open_decisions.decision: May a report be emailed to an address outside the client's own organization?
options: Yes, gated on the send-outside-the-organization privilege, held by Owner and Admin only
Yes, gated on that privilege, held by Owner, Admin and Engineer
No — recipients must be inside the client's domain in this release
open_decisions.recommended: Yes, gated on the send-outside-the-organization privilege, held by Owner and Admin only
open_decisions.consequences: The PRD files this as a leadership decision and leaves three cells of the privilege table unfilled pending it. It changes what a shared report means: an outside address reaches lenders, owners or auditors, and a file that has left cannot be recalled. Owner-and-Admin-only keeps the blast radius with the two roles that can already switch off somebody else's report, and still needs a visible per-address inside/outside marker in the recipient list. Including Engineer matches who may create and schedule reports, but puts un-recallable external delivery in the hands of the widest role. Refusing outside addresses entirely is the safest and removes both the privilege and the marker from this release — at the cost of the audit and lender reporting the PRD hints the account wants.

open_decisions.decision: Does a Technician get reports at all? Three cells of the privilege table are deliberately unfilled — see system reports, create a private report, and read run history.
options: No to all three — a Technician has no reporting surface at all
Read-only — see system reports and read run history, but cannot create
Yes to all three — a Technician may see system reports, create a private report, and read history for reports they can see
open_decisions.recommended: Read-only — see system reports and read run history, but cannot create
open_decisions.consequences: The PRD calls this a product question rather than a technical one: a Technician sees only assigned sites and manages nobody. This is the decision that determines how much the hidden-not-disabled rule actually has to do — with a no-to-all Technician, the setup page must render with no system tab, no create affordance and no history, and the layout must still not leave a hole, which is the most demanding version of REQ-50 and worth designing against deliberately. Read-only gives a Technician the reports Sand ships for their assigned sites without any authoring surface. Yes-to-all makes the Technician column identical to Engineer for everything except sharing, which weakens the reason for having the row.
